lessons.title: Sampling Techniques for Blends
lessons.body: Sampling is the first step in quality control. If you take a bad sample, all your lab results will be wrong, and you might reject a good batch or sell a bad one. For blended fertilizers, you need a sample that represents the whole batch. Use a sampling spear or a clean plastic scoop. For a pile of 1 tonne, take at least 10 random samples from different depths and positions. Mix them in a clean bucket, then quarter the sample until you have about 500 grams for the lab. For bags, take samples from at least 5% of the bags, up to a maximum of 20 bags. Use a bag trier to pull material from the top, middle, and bottom of each bag. Never sample from the surface of a pile because moisture and fine particles settle differently. In Africa, where humidity is high, take samples early in the morning when it is cool. Put samples in airtight plastic bags or glass jars, label them with batch number, date, and time, and send them to the lab within 24 hours. If you cannot send immediately, store in a cool, dark place. Remember, a sample is like a fingerprint of your batch. Take it right, and you can trust your results.

lessons.title: Laboratory Analysis: N, P, K, and Micronutrients
lessons.body: Laboratory analysis tells you exactly what is in your blend. For nitrogen (N), the most common method is the Kjeldahl digestion, where the sample is digested with sulfuric acid and a catalyst, then distilled and titrated. For phosphorus (P), use the spectrophotometer after extracting with citric acid or ammonium citrate. For potassium (K), use a flame photometer or atomic absorption spectrometer after extracting with ammonium acetate. Micronutrients like zinc, boron, and iron are measured using atomic absorption or ICP-OES. In many African labs, you can send samples to national agricultural research stations or private labs for a fee. For a basic N-P-K analysis, expect to pay around $30-$50 per sample. If you cannot afford a lab, you can use a simple field test kit for N, P, K, but these are less accurate. Always run a blank and a standard with known values to check your results. For example, if your standard says 10% N and you get 9.5%, your method is working. Record all results in a logbook. If your blend is supposed to be 20-10-10 and you get 19-9-9, that is acceptable if within 5% relative. But if you get 15-5-5, your batch is off and needs correction. Regular analysis builds trust with farmers and regulators.

lessons.title: Moisture and Particle Size Analysis
lessons.body: Moisture and particle size affect how fertilizer behaves in storage and in the field. Too much moisture causes caking, which makes spreading difficult and can lead to nutrient loss. To measure moisture, use a moisture meter or the oven-drying method. For oven-drying, weigh 10 grams of sample, dry at 105Â°C for 2 hours, cool in a desiccator, and weigh again. The weight loss is moisture. For blended fertilizers, aim for less than 2% moisture. If it is higher, you need to dry the blend or add a drying agent like diatomaceous earth. Particle size is measured using a set of sieves. Stack sieves with mesh sizes 1mm, 2mm, 4mm, and a pan. Shake for 5 minutes, then weigh the material on each sieve. A good blend should have 90% of particles between 1mm and 4mm. If you have too many fines (less than 1mm), the blend will dust and segregate. If too many large particles (over 4mm), it will not spread evenly. In Africa, where many farmers use manual broadcasting, uniform particle size is critical. Adjust your granulator or mixer if the size distribution is off. For example, if you find 30% fines, add a small amount of water and re-granulate. Test every batch and keep records. This simple test can save you from customer complaints.

lessons.title: Statistical Process Control
lessons.body: Statistical Process Control (SPC) uses data to keep your production consistent. You do not need a degree in statistics. Start by measuring one key quality parameter, like N content, for every batch. Plot the results on a control chart. Draw a center line at your target, say 20% N, and upper and lower control limits at Â±5% (19% and 21%). If a point falls outside these limits, stop and investigate. Also look for trends: seven points in a row above the center line means something is drifting. Use a simple calculator or a spreadsheet. For example, if your last 10 batches had N values of 19.8, 20.1, 20.3, 19.9, 20.0, 20.2, 20.4, 20.1, 19.7, 20.0, the process is in control. But if you see 21.5, that is out of control. Common causes of variation include inconsistent raw materials, worn mixer blades, or wrong weighing. In Africa, where raw materials vary, SPC helps you adjust quickly. Train one person to record data and plot charts weekly. Review the charts in team meetings. Over time, you will reduce waste and produce a more reliable product. Remember, SPC is not about punishing workers; it is about finding and fixing problems in the system.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Traceability
lessons.body: Record keeping is your memory. Without it, you cannot trace a problem back to its source. For every batch, record: date, time, batch number, raw materials used (supplier, lot number, amount), equipment settings, operator name, and all quality test results. Use a simple logbook or a spreadsheet. In Africa, where mobile phones are common, you can use a free app like Google Sheets or a notebook. Keep records for at least two years. Traceability means you can follow a bag of fertilizer from the factory to the farmer. If a farmer complains that his maize did not grow, you can check the batch record. Maybe the N was low, or the wrong raw material was used. With good records, you can identify the problem and recall other bags from the same batch. Assign a unique batch number to every production run. Write it on the bag and in the logbook. For example, batch 2025-03-15-01 means March 15, 2025, first batch. If you buy raw materials, keep supplier invoices and certificates of analysis. This helps if a supplier sends bad urea. In many African countries, regulators require traceability for fertilizer registration. Good records also help you improve. You can compare batches and see what works. Start simple: a notebook and a pen. But be consistent.

lessons.title: Handling Non-Conforming Product
lessons.body: Non-conforming product is any batch that does not meet your quality standards. It could be low nutrient content, high moisture, wrong particle size, or contamination. When you find non-conforming product, do not sell it. First, isolate it. Mark the bags clearly with a red tag or tape and move them to a separate area. Then investigate the cause. Was it a weighing error? A mixing problem? A bad raw material? Use your records to trace back. Once you know the cause, decide what to do. Options: rework (add nutrients and re-blend), downgrade (sell as a lower grade if allowed), or dispose of safely. For example, if a batch has 15% N instead of 20%, you can add more urea and re-blend. But if it is contaminated with oil, you must dispose of it. Never dump fertilizer in a river or on bare ground; it can pollute water. In Africa, some companies sell non-conforming product at a discount to local farmers, but this can damage your reputation. Better to rework or dispose. After handling, document everything: what was wrong, what you did, and who approved it. Then take corrective action to prevent it happening again. Maybe you need to calibrate your scale or retrain your operator. Handling non-conforming product well shows you care about quality.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Quality Control and Assurance in Fertilizer Blending

In African fertilizer blending operations â from the bustling blending plants of Kenya's Nakuru corridor to Nigeria's sprawling agro-dealer networks and Zambia's emerging blending hubs â quality control is not a laboratory luxury. It is a commercial survival tool. A single off-spec batch of NPK 23:21:0+4S delivered to a 500-hectare maize farm can destroy a dealer's reputation, trigger regulator sanctions, and lock a blender out of a regional tender worth millions of dollars.

This Practical Reference compiles the essential QC protocols, sampling standards, and documentation practices that African blenders need to operate profitably and compliantly. It draws on the AfricaFertilizer.org framework, the African Fertilizer and Agribusiness Partnership (AFAP) quality guidelines, and international standards adapted for African operating conditions.

Why QC Pays: The Business Case

Quality failures cost money at every stage. Re-blending a rejected 20-tonne batch costs US$3,000â5,000 in labour, lost materials, and downtime. A product recall across three districts can exceed US$50,000. More critically, in markets where farmer trust is the primary sales asset, a single nutrient-deficient batch can erase years of brand-building. Conversely, blenders with certified QC systems â ISO 9001, or national bureau of standards certification â consistently win institutional tenders from organizations like the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA), the African Development Bank, and national input subsidy programmes.

Sampling Techniques for Blends

Sampling is the foundation of all QC. A perfect laboratory analysis of a poorly drawn sample is worthless. In African blending plants, the most common sampling errors are insufficient increment numbers, contaminated sampling tools, and improper sample reduction.

Key principles:

  • Increments: For a 50-tonne batch, draw a minimum of 10â15 increments from different bag positions (top, middle, bottom) and different locations in the pile. Use a slotted probe or thief sampler.
  • Composite sample: Combine all increments, mix thoroughly on a clean, non-absorbent surface, and reduce by quartering to obtain a 1â2 kg representative sample.
  • Sample splitting: Divide the composite into three portions: one for analysis, one for the customer/regulator, one retained for 6â12 months.
  • Labelling: Every sample must carry batch number, date, time, sampler name, product specification, and intended destination.

For blended products, segregation is a real risk. Granule size and density differences cause N, P, and K particles to separate during handling. Sampling from the final bagged product â not just the blender discharge â is essential to detect segregation.

Table 1: Recommended Sampling Frequencies for African Blending Operations
Material / Stage Sampling Frequency Minimum Increments Sample Size
Incoming raw materials (urea, DAP, MOP, etc.)Every truck / 20 t lot102 kg
Blender discharge (bulk)Every 5 t during production81 kg
Bagged final productEvery 50 bags or 2 t122 kg
Retained samples (per batch)Each production batchâ1 kg
Moisture check (in-process)Every 2 hours3200 g

Source: Adapted from AFAP Quality Assurance Manual (2021) and ISO 8634:2022 â Fertilizers â Sampling of solid fertilizers.

Laboratory Analysis: N, P, K, and Micronutrients

A functional QC laboratory in an African blending plant needs, at minimum, the ability to determine total nitrogen, available phosphorus, soluble potassium, moisture content, and granule size distribution. Micronutrient analysis (Zn, B, S) is increasingly required for specialty blends targeting specific crops and soils.

Standard methods:

  • Total N: Kjeldahl digestion and distillation (AOAC 978.02) or combustion method (Dumas).
  • Available P: Spectrophotometric molybdenum-blue method after extraction in ammonium citrate or water (AOAC 963.03).
  • K: Flame photometry or atomic absorption spectrometry after dissolution (AOAC 983.02).
  • Micronutrients: ICP-OES or AAS after acid digestion. Zinc and boron are the most commonly specified in African blends.
  • Moisture: Oven drying at 105Â°C for 2 hours or moisture balance for rapid in-process checks.

Many smaller African blenders outsource analysis to national agricultural research institutes or university laboratories. Building even a basic in-house lab with a spectrophotometer, flame photometer, and drying oven typically costs US$15,000â30,000 â a worthwhile investment for plants producing above 5,000 tonnes annually.

Table 2: Typical Specification Tolerances for Blended Fertilizers in African Markets

Source: Compiled from Kenya Bureau of Standards KS 2295:2021, Nigerian Industrial Standard NIS 214:2018, and AFAP Regional Harmonization Guidelines (2023).

Moisture and Particle Size Analysis

Moisture and particle size are the two physical parameters most likely to cause caking, dust, and segregation â the "silent killers" of blend quality in humid African climates. High moisture (>2%) causes bag-set and caking, leading to customer complaints and product returns. Poor granule size distribution causes segregation during transport, so the farmer receives a product that no longer matches the label.

Moisture testing: Use a calibrated moisture balance or oven-drying method. In tropical conditions, test immediately after blending and again after 24-hour curing. Record ambient temperature and humidity alongside results.

Particle size: Perform sieve analysis using a set of standard sieves (1 mm, 2 mm, 4 mm). The target is typically 90% between 2â4 mm. Fines below 1 mm should not exceed 5%. Oversize above 4 mm should be crushed and re-blended.

â ï¸ Quality Alert: In high-humidity regions (coastal West Africa, Lake Victoria basin, Mozambique), moisture ingress during storage can push product above 3% within 72 hours. Always use moisture-barrier liners (PE or PP) and store on pallets, not directly on concrete floors. A blender in Tema, Ghana, reportedly lost a 200-tonne order to a cocoa cooperative when moisture-induced caking made the product unspreadable.

Statistical Process Control (SPC)

SPC transforms QC from reactive inspection to proactive control. By tracking nutrient content, moisture, and granule size on control charts (X-bar and R charts), blenders can detect drift before a batch goes out of specification.

Implementation steps:

  1. Establish control limits (Â±3 sigma) from at least 20 baseline batches.
  2. Plot each batch result on the chart immediately after analysis.
  3. Investigate any point outside control limits or any run of 7 consecutive points on one side of the mean.
  4. Document corrective actions and verify effectiveness on the next batch.

Even a simple paper-based SPC system, common in smaller African plants, delivers substantial value. Digital tools â including Excel templates and low-cost apps like QualiTrack â are increasingly accessible.

Record Keeping and Traceability

Traceability is both a regulatory requirement and a commercial advantage. In the event of a quality complaint, a blender with complete records can identify the affected batch, its raw material sources, production parameters, and distribution destinations within hours â not days.

Minimum records per batch:

  • Batch number and production date/time
  • Raw material lot numbers and supplier certificates of analysis
  • Blender settings (recipe, mixing time, temperature)
  • Sampling records and laboratory results
  • QC release signature and date
  • Distribution records (customer, quantity, date, destination)

Retain records for a minimum of 2 years â 3 years is better practice and often required for export or tender compliance.

Handling Non-Conforming Product

When a batch fails specification, the response must be immediate, documented, and decisive. Non-conforming product must be physically segregated, clearly labelled "HOLD â DO NOT SHIP," and quarantined in a designated area.

Disposition options:

  • Re-blend: If the deviation is minor (e.g., N is 0.6% below spec), re-blending with a high-N material may bring the batch into specification. Document the correction.
  • Downgrade: Sell as a lower-grade product if agronomically appropriate and legally permitted, with regulator notification.
  • Reprocess: Re-granulate or re-mix if physical properties are the issue.
  • Dispose: As a last resort, dispose according to environmental regulations. Never sell non-conforming fertilizer as compliant product.

Every non-conformance should trigger a root-cause investigation. Was it a raw material issue, a weighing error, a mixing problem, or a sampling error? The answer should feed back into supplier qualification, operator training, or process adjustment.

ð¨ SAFETY WARNING â CRITICAL: Fertilizer blending involves hazardous chemicals. Always wear appropriate PPE: dust mask (N95 or better), safety goggles, chemical-resistant gloves, and long-sleeved clothing. Ammonium nitrate-based blends are oxidizers and can become explosive if contaminated with organic matter or fuels. Never store ammonium nitrate near diesel, oil, or combustible materials. In case of skin contact with concentrated acids or bases used in laboratory analysis, flush immediately with copious water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention. Ensure adequate ventilation in the blending area and laboratory. Keep a material safety data sheet (MSDS) for every raw material on site, and train all staff on emergency procedures. In 2020, the Beirut port explosion â caused by improperly stored ammonium nitrate â killed over 200 people. African blenders must treat ammonium nitrate storage as a life-safety issue, not a paperwork exercise.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Raw material verification: Check supplier COA against specification before offloading. Reject or quarantine any material without documentation.
  2. Sampling discipline: Draw the correct number of increments, use clean tools, label every sample with batch ID, date, and sampler name.
  3. Laboratory turnaround: Analyse N, P, K, and moisture within 24 hours of batch completion. Do not release product without lab clearance.
  4. SPC monitoring: Plot every result on a control chart. Investigate any out-of-limit point or trend immediately.
  5. Moisture control: Test at blending and after 24-hour curing. Use moisture-barrier packaging and palletised storage.
  6. Traceability records: Maintain batch records linking raw material lots, production parameters, lab results, and distribution for at least 2 years.
  7. Non-conformance protocol: Segregate, label, investigate, and document every non-conforming batch. Never ship product on hold.
  8. Safety compliance: Enforce PPE use, maintain MSDS files, and audit ammonium nitrate storage monthly.

Further Reading

  • AfricaFertilizer.org â Continental platform for fertilizer statistics, quality guidelines, and country-level resources.
  • African Fertilizer and Agribusiness Partnership (AFAP) â Quality assurance manuals and training materials for African blenders.
  • ISO 8157:2021 â Fertilizers, soil conditioners and beneficial substances â Vocabulary â International standard for fertilizer terminology and classification.
  • FAO Fertilizer Statistics â Global and regional fertilizer consumption, production, and trade data.
  • African Development Bank â Feed Africa Strategy â Policy and investment context for fertilizer sector development in Africa.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme. For practical exercises, download the batch record template and SPC chart templates from the course resources section.

quiz.q: What is the first step in quality control for fertilizer blends?
quiz.explanation: Sampling is the first step because a bad sample leads to wrong results.

quiz.q: How many random samples should you take from a 1-tonne pile of blended fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: At least 10 random samples are needed to represent the whole batch.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to sample from the top, middle, and bottom of a bag?
quiz.explanation: A bag trier is designed to pull material from different depths in a bag.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid sampling from the surface of a fertilizer pile?
options: B) Moisture and fines settle differently
D) The surface is always dry
quiz.explanation: Surface material may not represent the whole pile because of segregation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage time for samples before sending to the lab?
quiz.explanation: Samples should be sent within 24 hours to avoid changes in composition.

quiz.q: Which method is commonly used for nitrogen analysis?
quiz.explanation: Kjeldahl digestion is the standard method for nitrogen determination.

quiz.q: What instrument is used for potassium analysis?
quiz.explanation: Flame photometer or atomic absorption spectrometer is used for potassium.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost for a basic N-P-K lab analysis per sample in Africa?
quiz.explanation: A basic N-P-K analysis typically costs around $30-$50 per sample.

quiz.q: Why should you run a standard with a known value during lab analysis?
quiz.explanation: A standard helps verify that the method is working correctly.

quiz.q: If your target is 20-10-10 and you get 19-9-9, what should you do?
quiz.explanation: A 5% relative deviation is often acceptable in fertilizer quality control.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended moisture content for blended fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Moisture should be less than 2% to prevent caking and nutrient loss.

quiz.q: Which method is used to measure moisture by oven-drying?
quiz.explanation: Oven-drying at 105Â°C for 2 hours is the standard method.

quiz.q: What size range should 90% of particles fall into for a good blend?
quiz.explanation: Particles between 1 mm and 4 mm ensure good spreading and minimal segregation.

quiz.q: What problem can too many fines (less than 1 mm) cause?
quiz.explanation: Fines cause dust and segregation, leading to uneven application.

quiz.q: Which sieve sizes are used for particle size analysis of fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Common sieve sizes for fertilizer are 1mm, 2mm, and 4mm.

quiz.q: What does Statistical Process Control (SPC) help you do?
quiz.explanation: SPC uses data to monitor and maintain consistent quality.

quiz.q: On a control chart, what does a point outside the control limits indicate?
options: B) Process is out of control
quiz.explanation: Points outside control limits signal a special cause that needs investigation.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of variation in fertilizer blending?
quiz.explanation: Variation in raw materials is a common cause of process variation.

quiz.q: How many points in a row above the center line suggest a trend?
quiz.explanation: Seven consecutive points on one side of the center line indicate a trend.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of record keeping in fertilizer blending?
options: B) To trace problems and improve
quiz.explanation: Records help trace issues back to their source and enable improvement.

quiz.q: How long should you keep batch records?
quiz.explanation: Records should be kept for at least two years for traceability.

quiz.q: What does traceability allow you to do?
options: A) Follow a bag from factory to farmer
quiz.explanation: Traceability lets you track a product through the supply chain.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you find non-conforming product?
options: C) Mix it with good product
quiz.explanation: Isolate non-conforming product to prevent accidental sale or mixing.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe way to handle non-conforming fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Reworking or safe disposal prevents environmental harm and protects reputation.

quiz.q: What is a corrective action after finding non-conforming product?
quiz.explanation: Corrective actions like calibration or training prevent recurrence.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label samples with batch number and date?
quiz.explanation: Proper labeling ensures traceability and accurate record keeping.

quiz.q: What is the acceptable relative deviation for nutrient content in many quality control programs?
quiz.explanation: A 5% relative deviation is commonly accepted in fertilizer quality control.

quiz.q: Which of these is a micronutrient often analyzed in fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Zinc is a micronutrient, while N, P, and K are macronutrients.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a desiccator in moisture analysis?
options: B) To cool the sample without absorbing moisture
quiz.explanation: A desiccator prevents moisture absorption while the sample cools.

quiz.q: What should you do if your blend has 30% fines?
quiz.explanation: Adding water and re-granulating can reduce fines and improve particle size.
